The faber CLI

Faber build tool#

The faber CLI is the primary entry point for building, checking, running, formatting, and testing Faber source. It wraps the Radix compiler into an ergonomic developer tool.

Core commands#

CommandPurpose
faber build <path>Compile a package to a target backend (default: Rust)
faber check <path>Type-check without emitting code
faber run <path>Run a source file, package, or archive: compiled in memory with Cranelift (clif-jit) when that lane accepts it, otherwise on the MIR runner; --target picks the engine
faber test <path>Run test cases on the MIR runner
faber format <path>Report files whose layout differs from canonical formatting; --write applies it
faber convert <path> --to <locale>Convert source between reader-locale surfaces (report-only unless --write)
faber explain <term>Explain a glyph, keyword, grammar term, or diagnostic code
faber emit <path>Compile to a target surface for stdout
faber targetsShow supported targets and capability notes
faber updateCheck for (--check) or install a newer release; --version <V> switches to an exact version, rolling back included
faber versionsList the installed versions and the active one
faber initCreate a new Faber package
faber replInteractive MIR runner REPL
faber verify <file>Run aspect verification on a single file
faber verify-library <input>Verify a library package's target binding manifest
faber model inspect <path>Inspect model-file metadata (safetensors)
faber lex / parse / hir / mir / cli-irJSON phase dumps (compatibility aliases for radix <phase>)
faber host manifestScript host introspection (kernel manifest)

Building a package#

faber build my-package/ -t rust

The -t flag selects the codegen target. faber build --help lists the accepted values and faber targets shows each target's current capability notes. Diagnostics can be promoted to errors with --deny-warnings (all warnings) or --deny <CODE> (a specific catalog code, repeatable).

Device execution (Metal / CUDA)#

faber run can execute a package's device program on a real GPU. A package carries a device program when its source declares a kernel and its manifest declares a [device] section (device, and inputs for the kernel's input buffers):

faber run --device metal <package>   # Apple Metal (e.g. Apple M5 Max)
faber run --device cuda  <package>   # NVIDIA CUDA (e.g. RTX 5070)
faber run --device auto  <package>   # resolve: exactly one admitted device
faber run --device reference <package>  # plain sequential code on the MIR runner
faber run --device cpu   <package>   # processor cores as a device

reference is the oracle that device results are checked against: the kernels run as ordinary functions, single-threaded, on the MIR runner. Since 1.17 cpu is a separate device. It goes through the same session and launch pipeline as metal and cuda, and a multicore worker queue runs the kernels. --threads N (or [device] threads) sets the worker count, and --partitions N selects partitions. A package without kernels runs on the reference route. Device selection precedence: CLI --device > manifest [device] device > auto. The packaged FMIR image's device section carries the canonical device program plus Metal MSL and CUDA PTX artifacts (each with a provenance hash); faber run drives a real Metal/CUDA session (load → allocate → copy-in → launch → sync → readback → release) and reports the selected device, the artifact/module hash, and the observed outputs. An explicit GPU request never silently falls back: unavailable backends, bad descriptors, and entry/dtype/shape mismatches fail closed with a stable code (E_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE, E_DEVICE_*, E_NO_DEVICE_PROGRAM).

Kernel integers. Since 1.17 a kernel may use int (64-bit), i64, u64, wrapping<u64>, saturating<u64> and d64 as values: parameters, tensor elements, lane binders, locals and stores. faber check stays clean, and the old SEM008 nucleum_wide_integer and nucleum_d64 refusals are gone. Whether a device can carry them is a per-target fact in the requirement report: Metal does; the other device targets refuse the kernel by name rather than approximate it. An integer intermediate beyond the 64-bit range (a d64 intermediate beyond its 128-bit carrier) is SEM008 nucleum_wide_intermediate, and f64 is still refused in kernels (SEM008 nucleum_f64). Write i32 and f32 to keep a kernel portable to every device:

@ public
kernel scale(tf32[4] a, i32 k) → tf32[4] {
    return a * (k ↦ f32)
}

Kernel safety tiers#

A kernel runs at one of three ordered safety tiers. The tier word follows the parameter list of the kernel head (la relaxed, unsafe):

TierWrittenFloat mathIndex checks
defaultkernel name(…)IEEE-correct; FMA contraction, reordered reductions and library transcendentals within their published boundsevery check the compiler cannot prove stays
relaxedkernel name(…) relaxedadds approximate / and sqrt, fast transcendentals, flushing denormals to zero and reassociating float expressionsas default
unsafekernel name(…) unsafeincludes relaxedalso drops the checks the compiler cannot prove; an out-of-range access is undefined behaviour
@ public
kernel scale_default(f32 x) → f32 {
    return x * 2.0
}

@ public
kernel scale_relaxed(f32 x) relaxed → f32 {
    return x * 2.0
}

@ public
kernel scale_unsafe(f32 x) unsafe → f32 {
    return x * 2.0
}

The tiers are one ordered choice, not independent flags: a head takes one mode word, and the annotation form @ kernel relaxed unsafe is refused (`PARSE018 duplicate_nucleum_tier), as is a tier on a fragment`, on anything that is not a kernel function, or a word that is not a tier. Integer results stay exact at every tier, and a check the author wrote (a trapping store, an is_finite test, a bounds test) always runs. On Metal the default tier emits IEEE division, precise sqrt and precise transcendentals, and the relaxed and unsafe tiers emit the fast forms. Since 1.18 CUDA selects f32 division and sqrt by tier too: correctly rounded at the default tier, approximate only at relaxed and unsafe. A backend that cannot honour a tier runs the default one, never a looser one.

faber run --safe and faber build --safe run every kernel at the default tier for that command, and safe = true under [device] in faber.toml does the same for the package. The switch can only lower a tier, and no environment variable sets it. Use it to check whether a relaxed or unsafe kernel changes an answer.

Kernel eligibility and --device-mode#

--device-mode is a compilation option on faber check, faber build and faber run. It decides which proofs the compiler may use for device code; --device still decides where a program runs.

faber check my-app/ --device-mode eligible
faber build my-app/ --device-mode eligible
faber run my-app/ --device metal --device-mode eligible
Callexplicit (the default)eligible
A host call outside do eligibleHostHost
A host call inside do eligibleHostA device candidate, launched once every check passes; otherwise host
A kernel calling an unmarked functionCompile error naming the dependencyCompiled when the function and its callees are proved device-safe
Anything a kernel or do device needs that is host-onlyCompile errorCompile error

The compiler infers eligibility for every function in both modes, and faber check --device <device> reports it as one INFO001 device_eligibility line per callable (--json gives JSON Lines). eligible mode moves no host code to a device outside a do eligible block, and it never excuses an unsafe body. Do eligible has the block's rules.

Device output and exit status#

Since 1.18 the device: selected backend line goes to standard error, so standard output carries only what the program prints. A kernel fault exits with the same status on every device as on reference: 70. The host no longer waits on each launch, so a fault can reach the program at the first read of that kernel's output, before later program output.

faber run --stats and --stats-file report the device buffer counters under device.runtime: allocations, releases, pool hits, and the buffers and bytes parked in the pool. A steady kernel loop, the same kernels at the same shapes, makes no device buffer allocations or releases once it has warmed up. The first iterations of a shape can allocate; a new shape can allocate once, then settles again.

Updating faber#

faber update --check reports whether a newer public release exists. faber update installs it under a versioned name (faber-<version>) beside the running binary and moves the faber link to it; --version <V> installs an exact version instead, which is also how you switch back to an older one. faber versions lists what is installed and which one is active.

faber update --check
faber update
faber update --version 1.15.1
faber versions

Checking without emitting#

faber check my-package/
faber check --lower my-package/

Runs the front end (lex → parse → semantic analysis) without producing output artifacts. Use this in CI and editor integrations.

Since 1.18 borrow-region inference is total. A construct it cannot yet reason about is refused by name (SEM008 region_facts_not_built) instead of being approximated.

--lower also lowers the program to Faber's reference form, without running it, and reports the errors that semantic analysis alone cannot see: a program that checks but cannot run. It needs a file or package path (not stdin). Since 1.16 it covers programs with command-line (cli) surfaces too.

Running tests#

faber test my-package/
faber test . --filter smoke       # substring filter on case path or title
faber test . --include math       # load only *.proba sources matching a path pattern
faber test . --exclude 'nested/*' # skip *.proba sources matching a path pattern
faber test . --name my_case       # select by test name
faber test . --suite suite/path   # select by describe suite path
faber test . --tag slow           # select by tag modifier

faber test runs test cases on the MIR runner, whatever engine faber run would pick — no Cargo or rustc is invoked for the package, so no Rust toolchain is needed. Inline describe and test suites live alongside source code, and colocated *.proba files are discovered as test-only sources (never imported, excluded from Cista snapshots). See Inline testing.

Formatting#

faber format my-package/

Runs the canonical Faber formatter, a HIR re-emit at the source file's own reader locale. By default it only reports each file that would change and exits 1 if any would. --write applies the change, --check is the explicit spelling of the default, and --stdout writes the result to stdout instead. Formatting never translates between reader locales; use faber convert --to <locale> for that.

Range glyphs come out space-padded, 0 ‥ 10, in value and type positions alike. Known issue in 1.18: faber format and faber convert print every kernel in the annotation form, @ kernel above an fn, so a kernel head does not survive --write yet. The result means the same thing.

Explaining diagnostics#

faber explain fn     # keyword reference
faber explain SEM001      # diagnostic explanation
faber explain ≡           # glyph reference
faber explain --search query

faber explain explains a Faber glyph, keyword, or grammar term, with diagnostic codes as a subset. It reads from the language corpus (radix/corpus/).

--locale <locale> chooses the reader locale whose spellings terms are listed and looked up by; without it faber explain uses the current package's faber.toml [locale], else English. --diagnostics-locale is separate: it sets only the message language of a diagnostic explanation.

The same split holds on every command. Since 1.18 --diagnostics-locale never changes how source is read, and faber build --locale applies to a single file and wins over its frontmatter. A frontmatter locale that is invalid or cannot be loaded is an error, not silent English: LOCALE003 on faber run, PKG001 on faber check and faber build.

In-process execution#

Alongside the compiled faber build path, faber run executes Faber source in this process, with no external toolchain.

Usage#

faber run script.fab

Since 1.18 this compiles the program to native code in memory with Cranelift, the clif-jit engine, and runs it. There is no object file, no linker and no rustc. When the Cranelift lowering declines the program, faber run falls back to the MIR runner, and the output is the same as --target runner. The choice is made before anything runs, so a program that traps or exits nonzero on clif-jit is never run a second time.

Device runs, archives, --stats and --shuffle-seed always use the MIR runner. --debug reports the engine on standard error, including when clif-jit declined the program.

Choosing the engine#

faber run --target <target> picks the engine and takes no fallback: a program the engine refuses stops with that diagnostic. runner and clif-jit run in this process. The others build the package for that target, then run the built program. Every engine takes the program's arguments after --, and the program's standard streams and exit code pass straight through.

--targetWhat it runsNeeds on PATH
runnerthe MIR runner, the reference every other target is checked againstnothing else
clif-jitnative code compiled in memory with Craneliftnothing else
tsa Node project, run with nodetsc and node
goa Go module (vendored runtime, builds offline), run as builtgo
llvm-hosta native program through LLVMllvm-as, opt, clang
faber run --target ts my-app/ -- --flag value
faber run --target runner my-app/

A missing tool is refused by name. faber build and faber emit refuse --target clif-jit and --target runner by name: those engines exist to run. Device packages keep their own route (--device, above).

How the runner works#

The compiler produces analysed HIR, validated MIR, and a resolved runtime-intrinsic table. The MIR runner dispatches MIR blocks straight to a host, skipping the wasm emit/instantiate round-trip:

Source → Lex → Parse → Collect → Resolve → Lower → Typecheck
                                                      ↓
                                                 MIR lowering
                                                      ↓
                                              MIR runner + Host

Latency#

The runner path runs the same linear frontend as the compiled path, plus runner time proportional to what the script actually executes:

PhaseCost
Frontend (100-line script)~0.6 ms
MIR steppingProportional to executed statements

The runner never invokes rustc or spawns a process, so startup is fast enough to feel like a shell script.

Limitations#

  • clif-jit has the language limits of the clif target, so a program it declines runs on the MIR runner instead
  • The MIR runner does not support all host I/O routes that the compiled path does — some norma:* wrappers remain compiled-only
  • The runner is a MIR-native diagnostic/reference executor, not a production runtime for deployed applications
  • Package compilation through Cargo remains the widest package product path today (Rust projection); other targets are measured separately
